utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I be reminded -- it's now your turn for re-examination, Ms. Richterova. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, but there will be no re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There will be no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Any questions by you, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask one thing for clarification. In the cross-examination you answered the question, but only in a very brief way, if these armed vehicles would have come through the village after the attack and you said this didn't happen anymore, but in the examination-in-chief you mentioned something about the first day after the attack that these vehicles or such vehicles in fact came through and there was some expression of irony or something similar you said. You remember that? Can you maybe explain once more if they came back at least one time and what happened there.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the 5th of August, 1991, after the first attack with 82-millimetre mortar shells at 0600 hours, when the attack stopped at 10.00, those two JNA armoured vehicles started driving through the town again but they were stopped by a crowd of people because the people were up in arms. They were against it; the residents of Saborsko I mean. And from that time on they didn't drive through anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: On the same point, was it the people, the crowd, who laughed at them that prevented them from coming through again?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was they, the crew of the vehicles, who were leering at us, the crowd, the crew of those two JNA transporters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you spoke earlier in your evidence about an armed clash in Plitvice. Who was this armed clash between? Who was engaged in this armed clash?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, 1991, it -- the first armed clash took place in Croatia between the Ministry of the Interior, the Republic of Croatia, and the so-called armed groups, renegade groups, in Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This was in Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The groups that you spoke about that cut off the Plaski and Licka Jesenica road, what ethnic groups were these persons?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms and JNA uniforms. They were putting up barricades, engaging in the so-called log revolution, and cutting off roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You spoke of a group of 100 men of the independent company of Saborsko and you said they came to defend, not to attack. Why do you say that they came to defend and not attack, and what form did this defence take?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not able to attack because they were coming to Saborsko, an occupied place, an encircled place. They were not attacking, they were defending, because Saborsko at the time was encircled. It was their homes we are talking about, their families. And that's why they came on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This is for my own education. You have spoken variously of Plaski and Plasko. Is it the same place? If not, please explain.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That group of 100 or 110 men - we've discussed this before - they were natives of Saborsko who were working in Rijeka or Zagreb and their families, wives and children were still in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Please go on to explain to me how that is related to Plaski and Plasko. I'd still like to hear if it's a different place or the same place or -- I am not understanding.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The name of the place is Plaski. There is only one place called Plaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is located between Ogulin and Saborsko -- or rather, between Josipdol, which is closer, and Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that 80 shells fell before 10.00, and it appears as if they didn't shoot right. And in the evening shells came to the centre of town. What sort of buildings and places were in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. The shelling started on the 5th of August, 1991 at 6.00 a.m., and Saborsko is at a higher altitude than Licka Jesenica. Maybe they didn't have the right coordinates so they didn't manage to hit Saborsko that morning. Their shells fell to the right of the church and the cemetery, that's if they were shooting at Saborsko at all. And towards the evening, they started hitting Saborsko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what sort of buildings were there -- or what was in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not actually a town; it's a village. In the centre there were schools, churches, family houses right along the road. The whole place is seven kilometres long all in all, and the houses line the road, the high street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said in Korenica you were beaten badly and cut in the face. Was anything said whilst you were being beaten or before you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much talking was done while the beating was going on. Yes, there were obscenities uttered. There was no personal talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: This is by the person or persons who beat you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening when they slashed my face with a knife and they knocked my teeth out, only one person was beating me while the others were standing around laughing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And this is a last question. You said you were told that it was your colleagues who were beating you. Who told you that it was your colleagues who were beating you, other detainees, the militia, or who told you such?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That was the military airfield Bihac on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The JNA military policemen said to take a group of five. We had been detained in the warehouse, and he told us: You are being beaten by your colleagues from Zagreb, renegades from the MUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. If I may just pick up from one of the questions that the Judge on my right asked. Would you like to show us the injuries that you sustained when they cut your face and broke your teeth?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour. Right here and they also slashed my face. My skin was black and the scars still remain, but since they slashed me on the head, I was already black and blue by that time so the scars are smaller. If they had slashed me now when my face is without any bruises, it would show differently. I don't know if you can see the scars, and the bridge of my nose was broken as well. It doesn't function really well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You mentioned in your testimony that around the 6th/7th of August, 1995, you returned to Saborsko and that when you got to Saborsko you found it overgrown and it was a ghost town. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That was the first time, Your Honour, that I came back to Saborsko after 1991. There was nothing to be seen in Saborsko except shrubbery and brush, burnt-down houses, and two heaps of rubble standing in the places where the church and the school building used to be. The houses were mainly wooden and burned down completely, and the rubble left over from the church was clearly visible. It is documented. There are photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what became of the population that used to occupy Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. We started looking for mass graves at that time because during the four years while Saborsko was occupied we were gathering information as to possible locations of those mass graves. And in 80 per cent of the cases, our operative information proved to be correct, the operative information we collected during the occupation. And we gathered it while we were in Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What happened to that population?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, after Saborsko fell on the 12th of November, 1991, they were killed and thrown into mass graves, into pits, or they were burned down together with their homes. There was several locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right at the beginning of your testimony you estimated the population at about 800 to 850 people. Am I to understand that you're saying the entire population was wiped out?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the populace fled. Those who were unable to flee, elderly men and women who remained, were killed, while those who fled ran through the wooded area called Kapela or in the other direction via Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the direction of Rakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I've understood you well, on the -- there was an attack around the 5th of August, 1991, and some people fled in buses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the 5th of August, while Saborsko fell on the 12th of November, in the autumn. But the first attack was on the 5th of August, and some people fled even then. The roads were still open for traffic at Slunj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now I understand. But you also testified that some of the people who fled on the 5th of August, 1991 returned?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those people came back. They had only fled to the neighbouring village of Rakovica, about 15 kilometres away along the forest-path, and they came back immediately. They ran away in the night of the 5th and came back on the 6th, because the place had not yet fallen, had not yet been occupied by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I understand you to be saying when Saborsko fell on the 12th of November, some people fled, some were killed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those that fled? Where are they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ran to Karlovac, some to Zagreb, some to Ogulin. They went to live there because Saborsko was occupied for four years. It was under the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina all the way until the military police Operation Storm. So they were absent from Saborsko from November 1991 until 1995. In that period, they stayed in the free territory of the Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, Rijeka, Karlovac, and then some went to third countries of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After 1995, where did they stay?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995, exhumations started and the restoration of the village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt --

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- some people returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Some of those people who fled returned. Okay. Now, you also talked of an attack on Rakovica. Do you know -- did you know the population of Rakovica before it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population of Rakovica was mostly Croat. There was some Serbs, too, but the majority were Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. All I'm -- do you know the numbers? Are you able to estimate the population in Rakovica before the attack?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That's a neighbouring place; it's larger than Saborsko. I don't know what its population was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you said it was partially destroyed. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's not 100 per cent destroyed, like Saborsko; it was destroyed 60 to 70 per cent maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any knowledge as to -- or an estimation of the number of people killed in Rakovica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about the number of killed in Rakovica and neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You talk of neighbouring villages. Were there any other neighbouring villages which were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The neighbouring villages were not destroyed at the time because in that area there are some villages and hamlets populated by Serbs, at least they were populated by Serbs in 1991, so they were not destroyed at the time. The only thing that was destroyed were Serb houses in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Serb houses in Saborsko. Okay. We have discussed Saborsko. What I do want to find out from you is: Are you aware of any other surrounding villages around Saborsko, Rakovica, which were also destroyed, and if so, what are they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that because I didn't live in those places, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, thank you so much. Any re-examination -- questions arising out of the questions from the --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I have a couple of clarifications. Further examination by Ms. Richterova:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, to the question of Judge Nosworthy you were talking about clashes in Plitvice and you stated: This first clash occurred on 1st of August. Previous in your testimony you mentioned 1st of April. When these clashes -- first clashes in Plitvice took place?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was a slip of the tongue. The 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other question was about your beating in Bihac, and that you were told that your colleagues from Zagreb did the beating. What did you understand when told your colleagues were those who beat you? Who were these colleagues? Were they Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were colleagues, Croatian policemen of Serb ethnicity, who had left, who, rather, became renegades vis-a-vis Zagreb. So they went to the Bihac airport Zeljava, so these are these four or five former colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question you answered to Judge Moloto that Serb houses in Saborsko were destroyed. How many Serb houses were there in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Saborsko there were four Serb houses, four family houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all these four houses destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that were down by the road itself were destroyed. Those are the houses that were destroyed. I don't know about one particular house which is further up, whether it was destroyed or not. But the ones down there were destroyed, torched and burned down. So I know this particular one where the family got killed, and they actually went to stay with my aunt and uncle and that's how I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the 12th of November, 1991, in the morning hours when the fall actually took place. I was not there, but then later on I learned from people that on the morning of the 12th of November, 1991 the attack started at 0900 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has just a few short questions. Further cross-examination by Mr. Milovancevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were answering the questions of the Prosecutor during this additional examination about your colleagues from Zagreb who beat you, that was the explanation that you were given. You said that these were people who were renegades from the MUP of Croatia. Can you say whether at that moment when you were at the airport belonged to the civilian or military police?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the statement made by the military policeman who was on duty at Zeljava airport, the military airport of Zeljava that is, he's the one who told us that they were our colleagues, these five who were walking around the airport and the barracks, and they beat not only me but other prisoners as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm asking you the following: At that moment, did they belong to the army or the police? They were at a military facility. An airport, an airfield is a very well-guarded area. Is it a military area? Were they civilians or military people?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The airport was not a well-guarded military zone. There were groups of Martic's men there. There was the JNA there. There were all sorts of things there. It wasn't only military policemen there. I don't know what. So there was a mix, and that's where they beat us. And we sang songs there in the warehouse, you know which ones, so it was not well-guarded at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just didn't answer the question. Do you know? If you do, you can tell us. If you don't, you can tell us that. At that moment these people left the MUP of Croatia, so were they in the police or in the military at that moment? If you know. If you don't, just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- well, they weren't in the police. They were in the military, in the army. The airport, Zeljava, is a JNA airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. When answering the questions of the Court as to what was in the centre of the village, you said the church and the school. Did you state yesterday that members of the special police of Duga Resa, who on the 5th of August, 1991, that is to say, the evening after this first attack, left Saborsko? Did you not say that they were staying at that school?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When responding to the additional question put by the Prosecutor a few moments ago, you said that these Serb houses in Saborsko were the first ones to be hit during the military operations. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he didn't say they were the first one to be hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to change my question or withdraw this question, if I misunderstood what the witness was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask you the following: Well, those were the first houses roughly that were burned. What did you mean? You said that there were a few houses by the road. Perhaps one was further up and you didn't know what happened to that, but your uncle and aunt came there and you gave some explanation what happened to these houses. Could you please tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness never said they were the first houses roughly that were burned. The word "first" was never used. I think rephrase the question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these Serb houses were destroyed. When and where and with what? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were destroyed in 1991, during the attack on Saborsko. So on the 12th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are these houses, in which part of Saborsko? What's the name of that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of Saborsko, that's where they are, and Borik is the name of that particular location, the hamlet of Borik. Together with Croat houses, too, not all of them were Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how they came to be damaged? I am not asking only about those Serb houses. It doesn't matter that they were Serb houses, but the houses where your uncle and aunt came, they are at the beginning of the village. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They're neighbours, my aunt's and uncle's houses at the beginning of the village, and then this other house that belonged to Selaja, also at the beginning of the village. So these are two neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of the houses destroyed that morning?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the houses were destroyed that morning during that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that your aunt and uncle came to those Serb houses that morning, to their neighbour's to seek protection, but nevertheless they fell victim?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they came to their neighbour’s. Now, did they go to seek protection or not? Well, neighbours are neighbours, but at any rate that is where they fell victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much, Mr. Vukovic. Thanks for coming to testify. You are free to go. Now you are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an oral application with respect to the next witness, but it requires us to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I be excused for five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And before we swear in the witness, can we just deal with how we are going to sit for the rest of the day now that we have had an unexpected break. It is the suggestion of the Chamber that we sit now and break at 11.00 for 20 minutes; resume at 11.20 and break at 12.20 for another 20 minutes; resume at 12.40 and break at 1345. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. May the witness please take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. The -- I just need to -- I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But one aspect of the voice distortion is that when the witness is speaking, all other microphones need to be turned off in the courtroom otherwise it can pick up. So I just wanted to alert the Chamber to that. I've already told Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've all heard that. And may we please be vigilant to make sure that we turn off our microphones if we are not speaking and the witness is speaking. Let us deal when we are not speaking, turn it off. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting -- well, may the witness proceed with the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear and understand me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I can hear you and understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, before I begin asking you questions, I want to explain to you the protective measures that have been granted to you for purposes of this proceeding. The following measures have been granted: You will be referred to by a pseudonym during these proceedings and all other proceedings; your -- there will be face distortion of any broadcast of this proceeding; in addition, voice distortion has been granted so your voice will be distorted in any broadcast of this proceeding; and finally, if there is any discussion of details which might tend to identify you, that will be done in private session so that there will be no broadcast of that part of the testimony. Do you understand those protections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show you what we refer to as a pseudonym sheet, it's a -- and ask you to look at it. And can you tell us if that is your name, your date of birth, and place of birth on the sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the usher please show that to the Defence counsel and then to the Chamber. Could that be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could that be admitted into evidence under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be admitted into evidence under seal and may it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 267, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, for purposes of these proceedings, you will be referred to either as "Witness" or "MM-037." That's a number that we have given you as a pseudonym. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have some water there in front of you. Feel free to drink some water, and if you don't understand any question or you can't hear it, please let us know. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, your -- because you have testified in a prior proceeding, your evidence has been admitted by this Trial Chamber in its written form from the prior proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher I'd like to provide the Chamber - and Defence counsel already has it but I can provide an additional copy - of the witness's testimony from the prior proceeding. And could that be admitted into evidence, please, under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness's prior evidence please be admitted into evidence under seal and be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Witness, the result of this is that it will not be necessary to go through all of your evidence again because it has been admitted in written form. The purpose of you coming here today is -- I will ask you just a few -- very few questions to just clarify a few points from your testimony, and then the Defence counsel will have an opportunity to ask you questions as well as the Trial Chamber. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just so that everybody's able to follow clearly your evidence, what I'm going to do is read out a summary of your prior testimony. Now, obviously it is the prior testimony which is in evidence which governs, and the summary is simply for purposes of the Trial Chamber and the parties to be able to follow the questions further. So for this time while I'm reading the summary, all you need to do is just listen to the summary. And when the summary is finished, I will ask you just a few questions about your testimony before the Defence counsel asks questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the purposes of the very beginning of the summary I would ask that we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will continue with the summary. The Witness is an ethnic Serb. His evidence concerns the area around Saborsko, Licka Jesenica, and Plaski. I would again refer Your Honours to page 19 of the atlas, Exhibit 23. At some point after early 1991, the witness joined the SDS. Before 1991, relations between Serbs and Croats were good, but as time went on there was more fear and more tension. Serbs became afraid because of messages from the HDZ. At some point, the SDS in Knin organised a referendum about establishing the SAO Krajina. The witness testified that "ordinary people thought it was some kind of protection and that -- and that something would be established that would protect us. Well, to put it simply, that the Croatian authorities would not come to that area, that would be it." After the events in Plitvice in Easter of 1991, there was a breakdown in communication between the Serb villages and the Croat villages in the area. In the village of Plaski, there was a police station which was mixed, but most of the employees were Serbs. At some point in time, the Croat members of the police left and some went to Saborsko. The ones that were left -- the ones that left, I'm sorry, were replaced by Serbs. The chief of the police at that time was Dusan Latas. Some other men went to Knin for training, and when they returned they were called Martic's police. These Martic's police wore some camouflage uniforms and some blue uniforms, but they had badges of the police of the SAO Krajina and they had automatic rifles that were obtained from Knin. The commander of Martic's police was a man by the name of Medakovic. Another man with Martic's police in Plaski was Djuro Ogrizovic who engaged in acts of looting. The commander of the TO of Plaski was a man by the name of Nikola Dokmanovic, who had formerly been in the JNA. The weapons for the TO were supplied by the JNA. They were brought in by night in crates. The JNA ordered the TO members to burn the crates after the weapons were distributed. This occurred in September or October of 1991. After the weapons were distributed, uniforms were provided to the TO soldiers by the JNA. In October or November of 1991, the JNA sent 18 officers who took over command of the TO, organised it, and structured it into a brigade with battalions. The commander of the TO brigade was Petar Trbovic. When these officers arrived, the TO also received mortars and anti-aircraft guns, and the TO soldiers were trained in their use. The TO brigade had a warehouse with supplies that Martic's police would also obtain supplies from. Around the time period of November 1991, the witness was told that there were Croatian soldiers in Saborsko and that it was a major stronghold of Croat forces, but he did not know this for himself. The witness heard but, again, does not know for himself that the authorities in Plaski asked the Croat forces in Saborsko to have free passage along the road and that nobody would be attacked. There was only one road that went through Saborsko. He also heard that in the days before the attack on Saborsko there were attacks by Croat paramilitary forces on the military barracks above Licka Jesenica, where there was also a JNA fuel depot and that sometime before the attack on Saborsko, three Serbs were killed above Licka Jesenica. The witness participated in the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991. The operation was commanded by Cedomir Bulat from the JNA. The TO was attached to the JNA for purposes of the attack, and Martic's police also participated in the attack. Soldiers gathered in Licka Jesenica for the attack, and although the witness did not see Martic's police there because they were attacking from the other side, he later saw them in Saborsko. The soldiers were told that the attack itself was delayed because of what -- bad weather which prevented the planes from flying. The witness testified that he heard various reasons for the attack on Saborsko. The witness heard that the leadership wanted to have the roads opened and communication lines opened, and Cedomir Bulat explained that Saborsko had to fall in order to be able to link up the Serb lands. There were shortages of salt and fuel in Plaski which was cut off from other Serb areas in the SAO Krajina. Saborsko was first attacked by planes and by artillery fire, followed by an infantry attack. The witness does not believe that there was any resistance from Saborsko, and no Serb soldiers were killed during the operation to the witness's knowledge. When the witness reached the hamlets of Tuk, Dumencici, and Solaje, which are all hamlets of Saborsko, he saw that the houses were set on fire by Serb forces. He saw people setting the houses on fire, but he could not recognise who they were because of the distance. Later the witness entered Saborsko itself and saw that everything was on fire, but he did not see how they were set on fire. The church in Saborsko was still standing, though it may have been hit by a projectile. Two weeks to one month later, the church was mined and destroyed. The witness saw both soldiers and police in Saborsko when he entered on the 12th of November, 1991, and he saw two or three of Martic's police engaging in looting of a shop. Before entering Saborsko, the witness learned that Pero Krtan, a merchant, and two men who had been with him had been killed, and he heard that they were killed by Martic's police. He thinks - the witness, that is - that Krtan was killed because he had money and not because he was a Croat. Later, after the attack on Saborsko, both dead people and dead animals were buried using an excavator. The witness heard that there were approximately 20 people killed, but he does not know how they were killed and he did not see anybody killed or any of the bodies. Approximately -- after the attack, approximately 50 to 60 elderly Croat civilians from Saborsko were taken to a neighbouring Serb village where they were given tea and sandwiches. The next day they were put on buses and driven to the Croat-controlled area towards Ogulin. Other bigger Croat villages in the area, Rakovica and Slunj, later fell after the 12th of November, 1991. That is the end of the summary of the witness's testimony. I just would like to ask a few questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, first I want to ask you something about Plaski. Did there come a time when Plaski, the village or town of Plaski, separated itself from the municipality of Ogulin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: That area fell within the municipality of Ogulin. With the political events that were going on then, a rift started, and the decision was made for Plaski to separate from Ogulin municipality. And this imaginary separation line was drawn near Vojnovac village. Vojnovac village is approximately halfway between Plaski and Josipdol. It's a bit closer to Josipdol. The railway goes through there and it was some kind of natural separation line against Ogulin. And Josipdol is 30 per cent Serbian and 70 per cent Croat in terms of population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when Plaski separated itself from the municipality of Ogulin, did it form its own municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: At the outset, there were indications that Plaski was going to join Titova Korenica municipality, but that was physically impossible because they were separated by Saborsko and Poljanak and Plitvice as well, so it was physically impossible. The only real connection between them went through Saborski. So Plaski set up itself as a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was it called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was unclear. When Plaski set itself up as a municipality, what was the name of the municipality that it created?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Plaski municipality. And I think it was then that the Autonomous District of Krajina was proclaimed and Plaski municipality became one of its parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from the village of Plaski itself, were there other villages that became part of this new Plaski municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: This entire area, Vojnovac, Plaski, Blata, and Licka Jesenica, that entire area populated by Serbs, except for perhaps 2 per cent Croats, became part of that Autonomous Region of Krajina. There was maybe just one village that was purely Croat, and in Plaski there were plenty mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear: This -- these villages that you mentioned, Vojnovac, Plaski, Blata, Licka Jesenica, did these villages all become part of the Plaski municipality which -- which was a part of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was this Plaski municipality isolated in any way from the rest of the SAO Krajina, geographically speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think all that you read in the summary is quite accurate. Maybe Plaski is a bit out of that context and it's not quite clear -- sorry, what did you ask me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. I'll repeat my question. Just listen carefully to the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, I remember now. That new Plaski municipality was completely isolated because it was completely surrounded by Croat villages, and you couldn't leave Plaski, you couldn't go anywhere, without going through a Croat village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the first president of the Plaski municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: The first president was Nikola Medakovic nicknamed Medo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this the same Medakovic who was the head of Martic's police in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he hold both positions at the same time; that is, president of the municipality of Plaski and head of Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, at that time, at the beginning, it was a very small group. So he was simultaneously president of the municipality and headed that group of mainly very young men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These very young men, were those the Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could you describe for us please in October and November -- and this is to your knowledge. In October and November of 1991, what kinds of police existed in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: You see, I just want to say that throughout that time, from the beginning of the conflict almost until the end, until the Operation Storm, there were three kinds. The real police in 1990 and 1991. Plaski was the administrative centre of that area. However, after that time it became part of Ogulin district, and the police station of Plaski merged with the police in Ogulin. However, after these changes, the police station in Plaski, as an autonomous police station, was re-established and it had 10 to 12 policemen employed. In the very beginning of these events, several young men went to Knin, to Golubic more precisely, to get training. And when they came back, they started calling themselves the Martic police. When the peacekeeping forces came to the contact line, to the speculation line, the demobilisation of the Territorial Defence started. The police took up those positions, and they were paid policemen as well. When the peacekeeping forces came, all the battalions were disbanded and there remained only one police company that consisted of people who wanted to be policemen, although they received salaries. When Maslenica was attacked and when it fell, there was a new mobilisation of all military conscripts, and that's how it continued until the end. Those are the three police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you for that very complete answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When what was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe the witness said "Maslenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you made a reference to -- in explaining the third category, the third group, you made a reference to when the peacekeeping forces came. Was that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think so. I can't remember exactly. But what I was trying to say is this: The mobilised members of the Territorial Defence were released to go home. They were no longer part of the army. From the attack on Maslenica until the arrival of the peacekeeping forces, there was a police force who held the positions, and they were neither the Martic's police nor the regular police that we had at the beginning commanded by Latas. It was neither of these. The regular police did not return to Plaski, the regular police, you know the kind you go to when you need something. But when the peacekeeping forces, when they came, they demobilised us, the Territorial Defence, and we stayed at home until Maslenica fell. We were not militarily engaged. I don't know if I've managed to put it clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think so, but I just want to ask you a couple of questions to try to clarify it further. I want to focus on 1991. In 1991 - and more specifically in, let's say, September and October of 1991 - did there exist what you refer to as the regular police in Plaski, those you would go to if you needed something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there exist also what you've described as Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, but not the third one. That third one did not become active until the arrival of the peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that, to your best recollection, was sometime in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, sometime around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I think you've made it clear. So I'm going to focus my remaining questions on 1991, on just those first two groups, the regular police and Martic's police. You've already testified that Nikola Medakovic was the head of Martic's police. Who was the head of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Latas, Dusan Latas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've -- did both types of police, that is, the regular police and Martic's police, participate in the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you've already testified that you saw Martic's police in Saborsko. Do you recall if you also saw the regular police in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, they acted together from the same axis. They were given the assignment to act from the same axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "they were given the assignment," do you mean by that that both the regular police and Martic's police were given the assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think they were acting together in the attack on Saborsko because the main operation was led by the JNA. We were just attached to the battalions, resubordinated. The 25 or 30 of us were just attached to those battalions, whereas the main ground of the 5th Military District was precisely in our vicinity near Plasko. That was the headquarters of the entire 5th Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a question about Licka Jesenica. Was there a JNA barracks there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there also a fuel depot there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: It was actually a large fuel depot, a military one, and it was guarded by the army. The barracks provided security for that fuel depot because it contained large quantities of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In October and November of 1991, was this barracks, this JNA barracks and the fuel depot, were they blockaded in any way by Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: It was not a blockade in the traditional sense. Rather, Croat forces tried to take-over that depot because of course they wanted the fuel and they did not succeed. But there was no blockade in the traditional sense barring entry and exit; it was just an attack that was repelled. The purpose of the attack was to take over the depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that before the attack on Saborsko you were told that Saborsko was a Croatian stronghold. First of all, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: We spent an entire day and an entire night in Licka Jesenica before Saborsko was attacked, and by that time people were already nervous and -- about a mutiny. And Cedo Bulat then said that we were waiting for good weather for aircraft to be able to fly, because Saborsko was a very strong Croat stronghold, and that's why they didn't want to take any risks. They wanted aircraft support and they were waiting for good weather. It's difficult for me to explain this because I'm not a military expert, but they wanted, I think, the aircraft to go first and to use the heavy weapons first and then the infantry. However, the weather was tricky and he didn't want to try and attack Saborski without air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, from what you were able to see and learn during the attack, was that true? Was it a Croatian stronghold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I have a feeling that in view of the role of my group there was no strong resistance offered from Saborsko, not as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that the church was damaged or may have been hit by a projectile at the time of the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991, but that it was only destroyed some two weeks or one month later. How did you learn that it had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: That became common knowledge immediately. It was just hit with a tank shell, but the tower remained standing. Within 15 or a -- days or a month, the church in Saborsko was bombed and destroyed, but it didn't happen during the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see it after it was bombed and destroyed some 15 days or a month later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I passed through that area much later and I saw that all that remained of the church was a heap of rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have one last topic, and that is I'd like to show you a document which is 65 ter Exhibit 1258.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if that could be put up on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter, and if we could -- it's addressed to a Rudolf Spehar, and if you look at the bottom, if we can go down to the bottom, you see it's from Nikola Medakovic and it's dated the 13th of November, 1991. Now, you've already provided evidence about the -- who -- you've already told us who Nikola Medakovic was at that time. Do you know who Rudolf Spehar was at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: After the victory of the HDZ at the elections, the Croat Democratic Union, Spehar was a great activist in the area, and on that basis he became president of Ogulin municipality. I know the man personally because he was two years above me in the Ogulin high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, in the letter -- if we could scroll up on the B/C/S and -- there. Right there. Perfect. Do you see a sentence it says -- and on the English it's -- let me see if it's visible on the English one. Yeah. There's a sentence which says -- the letter is about the attack on the Saborsko. And it says -- there's a sentence which says: "The immediate cause for the attack were your soldiers' gruesome actions towards the civilians during the attack on Licka Jesenica." And then there's another sentence about that. Do you know what that is a reference to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I think those were the first casualties, victims in that area, three Serbs who went from Plaski to the neighbouring village to buy horses. So they took their tractor with a trailer and drove there, and as far as I know only one of them had a rifle. It is a 16-kilometre forest road from Licka Jesenica to Dabar. There is only one house on the way, and where the road forks towards Glibodol village they were ambushed and killed in a really atrocious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those Serb men, were they members of the TO in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, because they were rather young people. Everybody up to 60 years of age had the obligation towards Territorial Defence. They could be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we can just scroll down on the -- to the bottom of the document. You see that stamp there. Can you read what that stamp says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: "SAO Krajina Municipal Assembly of Plaski."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see that stamp on other documents at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the document please be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number 269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I want to thank you. Those are all my questions, and now it will be time for the Defence to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose it will be a convenient time to take the break. We will come back at 20 past 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, before we proceed, may I ask you to please slow down when you answer questions so that we can follow you. I think you speak a little too fast for us. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I finished my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You finished your questions. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic. It is even more important that you slow down because Mr. Milovancevic is probably going to be speaking the same language as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am Defence counsel for Milan Martic. Now we are come to the stage of your examination that is called the cross-examination. You should know about this. I am going to repeat this request. When a question is put, could you please pause before answering, and I will do the same thing, so the interpreters can interpret what is being said. So please speak slower. Another matter: Please do not mention job titles and things like that precisely because of these protective measures. When we get to things like that, we're going to ask for private session. You said in your statement that you worked in Plasko for many years and that you stayed at work until August 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry. There are two matters. First, I would just remind Defence counsel that he has to turn off his microphone after he asks the question. The second matter is: I think questions about the witness's job should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to go into private session, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I think that would be useful if we moved into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, before you proceed, there is a reference to Plasko. I would like to know: Is there a difference between Plaski and Plasko, because the -- the names seem to be used interchangeably, I want to know, or if it's two different places, Plaski, Plasko. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one and the same place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said in your statement to the Prosecution and during your testimony when you talked about the fear of the Serbs in 1990, you mentioned and you stated that this fear was based on recollections as to what happened to the Serbs during the Second World War and also that the Serbs were afraid of the Croatian government because of some of the statements that their politicians had made about Serbs in Croatia. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes. I said the following, quite literally: That when the HDZ won the democratic party elections in Croatia, that they -- had they had a different attitude towards the Serb ethnic being the situation would have probably been quite different from today. However, when the constitution of the Republic of Croatia was changed, the Serbs were not even mentioned in the constitutional preamble. It was said that the Croatian state was the state of Croat people and indivisible, and so on. And secondly, Croat officials were trying to outdo each other in terms of bad words about the Serbs. I think that it was Sime Djodan who said in 1941, and this was all over the media, and he said quite literally that Serbs in Croatia were a disruptive factor. For as long as they were there, Croatia would not be -- well, that they should be expelled, baptised, killed. So that led to this fear. Well, it wasn't easy for anyone to take up arms and nobody wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Sime Djodan made a statement that Serbs were a disruptive factor and that they should be eliminated from Croatia. During the Easter --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Message. I think it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can remember to pause after each question, you will automatically cover the switching off of the microphone. Please just pause. Don't rush to answer as soon as Mr. Milovancevic finishes asking the question. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the Trial Chamber told you that they had time to hear you. You don't have to hurry. We are not being asked to hurry, so please let me put my question. You said that Sime Djodan made a statement that Serbs in Croatia were a disruptive factor, that they should be converted, expelled or killed. You did not tell us who Sime Djodan was at the time. What was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: He was a member of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was a member of the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, but, but when I said that -- I mean, I said that for the following reason. I thought that such statements may -- did a great deal of harm to the Serb people and to the Croatian people. It led to a lot of fear. Things would have been different. The situation would have evolved differently had there not be such statements and such fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the fear of this population in the region of Plasko and you said that in 1941 they suffered badly. You talked about a pogrom, so was this a mass suffering and loss of life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, that is evident. This entire area, Kordun, Banja, Lika was afflicted very badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that during the war in 1941 the entire area of Banja, Kordun, and Lika was afflicted badly, what population was afflicted badly and by whose authorities, in order to make it clear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: The HDZ authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And what population -- what population was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, NDH, not HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of a statement made by the then-president of the HDZ and the future president of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, in February 1990 in the Vatroslav Lisinski hall in Zagreb when the HDZ was being established, that the independent state of Croatia is not only a fascist crime and a fascist creation but also an expression of the historic aspirations of the Croatian people. Have you heard of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that I particularly listened to that, but similar statements could often be read in the newspapers, too. But I could not remember that particular detail right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question in relation to this question. This statement made by Sime Djodan, then-high ranking politician in Croatia, was it the only statement of this kind or were there many such statements or were there a lot of such statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I mentioned this one because I personally read this one and remembered that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that kind of situation, elections were held, the first multi-party elections in Croatia in April 1990. And in your statement to the OTP you said that Serbs in Plasko voted for SDP. Can you give us the full name of that party and who headed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: SDP. Its full name is the Party of Democratic Changes headed by Ivica Racan. We saw it as the successor of the communist party, and we in our region had no one else to vote for and we thought they were the best option, so almost everybody voted SDP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the full name of that party was SDP, an acronym for Party of Democratic Changes - League of Communists of Croatia, and would I be right in saying that Ivica Racan was a politician of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm the communist party bit. It's just that we trusted Ivica Racan as a politician because he had been a politician for many years. He had been in the political arena of Croatia for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained the reasons for the fear of Serbs and the events of April. The first multi-party elections in Croatia were won by the Croatian Democratic Union headed by Mr. Tudjman, and after that some constitutional amendments were proposed. Is it the case that those constitutional amendments proposed that Serbs be deleted as a constituent nation from the constitution of Croatia and be renamed a national minority, that the Serb language be banned, and that Croat emblems and iconography be introduced? Was that the essence of the proposed constitutional amendments, and what was the reaction of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you're driving at, but it is my opinion that if there had been any political wisdom and if they had put it differently, namely, that the state of Croatia belonged to all peoples who inhabited it, things would have been much different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you just say that the Serbs reacted to the new formulation, stating that Croatia was a state only of its citizens of Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in 1990 at the elections in Plaski you voted SDP, the Party of Democratic Changes, headed by Mr. Ivica Racan. You said that at that time SDS did not have a presence in Plaski. In your statement to the OTP, this acronym "SDP" is explained as Serbian Democratic Party. Is that right? Is it the case, rather that its name was Party of Democratic Changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Party of Democratic Changes is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in how many municipalities in the then-Republic of Croatia did that party called SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, headed by Jovan Raskovic, win in 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think that that party arrived into our area rather late, too late for the elections; however, they did win in Knin and the surrounding area. In our area, we joined that party en masse but only after the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Many Milovancevic, your question said "party called SDS." Did you mean to say "SDP"? That last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. The witness was saying that the residents of Plasko voted SDP. And I then asked him what happened with the SDS party at the elections, how many votes they won in Croatia, in how many municipalities they won. So we were talking about an entirely different party, not the one the witness voted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would I be right in saying that SDS won in only four municipalities at those elections, Knin, Benkovac, Gracac, and Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Possibly. Because those places were closer to Knin where that party had a presence, so it's possible. I can't say one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you had voted for the Party of Democratic Changes, with the acronym SDP, headed by Ivica Racan at those elections in 1990, and only later did you move to SDS and Serbs en masse joined the SDS. Can you tell us why that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I think it was the personality of Jovan Raskovic that was the main reason, and if Jovan Raskovic had stayed in that party -- I had the opportunity of hearing his speeches many times. That man did not want war, and if he had stayed in that position, we would have avoided bloodshed maybe. And that's why many Serbs joined the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was Jovan Raskovic the president and the founder of the Serbian Democratic Party, SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, allow me to finish my question before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can I just -- may I also just remind you that you are actually -- this is a 92 bis witness and your cross-examination is supposed to be dealing with the questions relating to the Martic's police. I know that a few questions were asked this morning by the Prosecution, but I'm not getting the impression that you are dealing with those questions also -- either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about to move to that topic. I just wanted to provide a general picture of 1990 so that further comments would be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My next question to you, Witness, is: You voted en masse for SDS in 1990 and then many Serbs joined SDS instead, mainly attracted by the personality of Jovan Raskovic. Was he a man who, as a founder of the SDS, hated Croats or said anything against the Croats? Did anyone ever hear him talk about a plan to expel or kill Croats, to start a war or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the formulation of the question. It's impossible for the witness to answer. Did anyone ever hear him talk about these things? The witness is not capable of answering that question. All he can answer is what he heard about what Jovan Raskovic said or didn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the answer I expected to hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You joined Jovan Raskovic's party, attracted by his personality and his ideas. Did you ever hear him say anything of the kind I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I had a feeling that Jovan Raskovic wanted to avoid war at all costs. That's my conviction, my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a skirmish, an armed clash, in Plitvice in April 1991. What exactly happened at Plitvice; do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: From what I know, the area of Plitvice was already an imaginary border. It contained Licka Korenica, populated by Serbs and it was under Serb control. And the Croatian police then were sent there and a conflict occurred, including casualties, two casualties as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Did the Croatian police attack Serbs or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. I know that the area was controlled by Serbs, and as for who attacked --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the JNA intervened to separate the conflicting parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I don't know if the JNA was stationed there. I think they were. They probably stopped this clash. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You explained that Plaski was surrounded by Croat villages completely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: What I meant to say is that Plaski is geographically situated in a -- in an area filled mostly with Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask. The neighbouring villages around Plaski were populated mainly by Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after this, developments in Croatia in August 1991, Serbs organised themselves and attempted to create Plaski as a municipality. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, Plaski separated. I said that from the Second World War until 1964 Plaski was the administrative centre of that district. From 1964 onwards, it was merged with Ogulin municipality and it fell under Ogulin municipality. And then on the eve of these conflicts, it separated again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1964, was Plaski as a separate municipality mostly populated by Serbs or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: It had a majority Serb population, but it also included Saborsko village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So from World War II until 1964, Saborsko was a municipality with a majority Serb population. Are you now saying that -- sorry. I meant to say "Plaski." This was a slip of the tongue. Plaski was a municipality with a majority Serb population. And after 1964 it was re-organised to merge with Ogulin municipality. Was Ogulin a municipality with a majority Croat population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when these events were going on, the events we just discussed, is it the case that the Serb population of Plasko again tried to set their own municipality up, the municipality of Plaski --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could there just be clarification about what time period we're talking about? Because it -- I'm not clear if we're talking about -- what events we're talking about. Are we talking about Plitvice in April?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We are now talking, and even my last question referred to year 1991. You said you participated in the elections, you voted for SDP, that that was not a good idea, and the political developments made us turn towards the SDS, and Plasko separated itself from Ogulin and was set up as a municipality again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, although there's a bit of confusion. Parliamentary elections in Croatia were I believe in 1990. At that time there was not a single Serb political party in Plasko area yet, and we thought that SDP was somehow the most acceptable to Serbs. And that's why we voted for SDP. However, as things continued to develop, Serbs and Croats were increasingly being confronted and tensions rose. And you are confusing me with your questions about various periods. These developments led to an aggravation, an escalation of tensions, and the communication between Serbs and Croats was diminished out of fear. Croats were afraid to go to Serb places and vice versa. Only later when it became obvious that things were taking a very bad turn, Jovan Raskovic and his party appeared on the scene, and he held a rally in Plaski in 1990 perhaps, at the end of that year, and was met with great enthusiasm. We thought that thanks to the wisdom of Jovan Raskovic and his party, things would finally start to improve and we would be able to avoid all the things that eventually we were not able to avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You stated that sometime in end August or early September you were mobilised in the TO unit in Plasko, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a call-up paper? Who mobilised you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: At the beginning it was self-organisation of the people. People were afraid that Croatian authorities would send somebody to their area to -- those were all assumptions. Maybe that wouldn't have happened anyway. But the fear was there and people were organising themselves in order to defend themselves just in case. We didn't have any other weapons but hunting rifles, and we thought if the Republic of Croatia decided to use force to enter our area, there might be arrests. And that was our reasoning at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this mobilisation of the Territorial Defence was an attempt to self-organise for defence out of fear, that fear that pervaded the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: I'm going to try to explain this better. Those were first forms of self-defence inspired by that fear. We had among us Nikola Dokmanovic, a former JNA officer, an honourable man, who knew about these things and he became the leader of that Territorial Defence. Let me just explain this till the end so you don't need to ask me additional questions. At a later stage, the army began arming us. They would bring in weapons that would be distributed during the night, whole cases with weapons would be opened and distributed, and those were the first initial forms of self-organisation for defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you with a brief question. Do you know when it was that Croatia proclaimed secession from Yugoslavia? Was it on the 25th of June, 1991? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I cannot say. Well, I know that they proclaimed it -- well, I don't remember exactly when. I don't remember this detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I did not expect you to confirm the exact date, but I'm duty-bound to give you the exact date. So was this in June 1991, can you put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-037
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, something I would note. This question has been put to witnesses again and again. This specific question -- and this is also true of other questions. This is an agreed fact in the case. We've agreed on that fact, and so I'm not sure why it has to be put to witnesses for them to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Is that an agreed fact, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is an agreed fact but that doesn't mean that it is an unimportant fact. That is the most important fact for the Defence in relation to the Martic case. I put the question only to be able to get to the next question in relation to the events that the witness is talking about. So in this one sentence I wanted to make an introduction into what came next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
